intro: Looking for a commercial architect near you usually means you have a business premises to design, change or fit out, and you want someone local who understands commercial buildings. You might be opening a shop, reworking an office, converting a unit or planning an industrial scheme. We introduce you to a suitable UK architecture practice, and they quote you directly, so the price is on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a commercial architect usually need
need_lead: Commercial work has its own pressures, and the brief is usually shaped by how the building has to earn its keep.
needs: You are fitting out a retail unit or hospitality space and need the layout to work for customers, staff and deliveries.
You are refitting offices and want the space to suit how your team actually works now.
You have an industrial or warehouse scheme and need the shell and servicing thought through properly.
You are changing the use of a building and need help with planning permission and building regulations approval.
You need fire safety provisions designed in from the start, because the rules for commercial buildings are strict.
context: "Architect" is a protected title in the UK. Only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices.

Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, but they are not registered architects, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring. Before you appoint anyone, check the ARB register and ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe the type of building, whether it is a shop, office, restaurant or industrial unit.
Explain whether you are fitting out an interior, altering the shell of the building, or both.
Say where the property is, so we can introduce you to a practice that works in your area.
Set out what you want the space to do for the business, including how customers and staff will use it.
Mention whether you already have planning permission or building regulations approval, or still need them.
Note any programme pressures, such as a lease start date or a busy trading period you need to be ready for.
questions: Are you on the Architects Registration Board register, and can you confirm your professional indemnity insurance?
How will you approach fire safety for this type of commercial building?
Will you handle planning permission and building regulations approval on our behalf?
What is the difference in your approach between fit-out work and shell work for this project?
How will you keep the design within our business brief and any programme constraints?
Can you set out your services, fees and responsibilities in a written appointment before we start?

faqs.q: Do I need a registered architect for a commercial fit-out?
faqs.a: Not always, but "architect" is a protected title, so anyone using it must be on the Architects Registration Board register. Architectural designers and technologists can also do good work, so it is worth asking which you are hiring and checking the register.

faqs.q: Can an architect help with planning permission and building regulations?
faqs.a: Yes. Planning permission and building regulations approval are separate processes, and your architect can help you navigate both. Ask for this to be set out in the written appointment.

faqs.q: Why does fire safety matter so much for commercial buildings?
faqs.a: Fire safety rules are strict for commercial premises, and they affect layout, escape routes and materials. Raise this early with the practice so it is designed in rather than added later.

faqs.q: What is the difference between fit-out and shell work?
faqs.a: Fit-out covers the interior of a unit, such as partitions, finishes and services, while shell work concerns the structure and envelope of the building. Tell us which you need so we introduce you to a practice suited to it.

extra_heading: Choosing between local practices for commercial work
extra: Searching for a commercial architect near you narrows things usefully, because commercial projects often benefit from someone who knows the local planning authority and can visit the site without a long journey. Being close by also helps with site inspections during the build, when problems are easier to sort out in person.

When you compare practices, ask each one to talk you through commercial projects of the same type as yours, whether that is a shop, an office, a restaurant or an industrial unit. Listen for how they handle the business brief, fire safety and the difference between fit-out and shell work, and ask how they would keep the design within your programme.

Price is on application, so ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities before you commit. A local practice that explains its approach clearly and puts the commercial pressures of your project first is usually a better guide than distance alone.

extra_faqs.q: Does a commercial architect need to be local?
extra_faqs.a: It is not a requirement, but a practice near your premises can visit the site more easily and will often know the local planning authority. That can help during design and while the work is on site.

extra_faqs.q: How do I compare commercial architects near me?
extra_faqs.a: Ask each practice about its experience with your type of building, how it approaches fire safety and whether it will handle planning permission and building regulations approval. Ask for a written appointment setting out services, fees and responsibilities so you can compare like for like.

extra_faqs.q: What should I have ready for a first appointment?
extra_faqs.a: Bring whatever you have on the property, such as lease plans, existing drawings or a survey, and be clear about how the building needs to work for your business. It also helps to say whether you are fitting out an interior, altering the shell, or both.
